alalal-c49641-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 24: whether an angel's motion is in time or in the now.

alalal-c49641-d1e115.summary: States the third question on angelic motion: whether it is in time or in the now.

alalal-c49641-d1e122.summary: First argument for time: every motion has before and after as essential parts, and all before and after is in time.

alalal-c49641-d1e136.summary: Second argument: every motion is successive, existing in parts one after another, and whatever so exists is in time.

alalal-c49641-d1e154.summary: Third argument: Avicenna defines motion as the exit from potency to act in continuous time, not suddenly.

alalal-c49641-d1e167.summary: Fourth argument: Aristotle defines motion as the act of what is in potency as such, mixing act and potency in different respects; act as the way toward a terminus and potency as what it casts off. Casting off and acquiring are not simultaneous but in different parts of time, so no motion is in the now.

alalal-c49641-d1e215.summary: Fifth argument: if one angel moved in a now, a stronger angel would cross the same space in less than a now, which is less than an indivisible.

alalal-c49641-d1e237.summary: Sixth argument, against the earlier suggestion of three successive nows: between any two indivisibles of a genus lies a composite of that genus, as a line between points.

alalal-c49641-d1e266.summary: Seventh argument: between any two nows there is time, so three nows without anything between are impossible.

alalal-c49641-d1e278.summary: Eighth argument from Averroes on Physics VI: in every motion the moving thing is partly in the place it leaves and partly in the next, so there is always intervening space; all motion is divisible with space, and so its time is divisible, and no motion is in a now or consists of successive nows.

alalal-c49641-d1e320.summary: Reports an opposing view: where there is no medium, becoming and having become are simultaneous, as in simple substantial generation between contradictories; its proponents use this to argue that the angel's moving and having moved are simultaneous, though they do not prove it.
concepts: simultaneity of fieri and factum esse

alalal-c49641-d1e353.summary: Offers an argument for that view: as qualified generation is from qualified non-being, simple generation is from simple non-being, i.e. from nothing; between nothing and something there is no medium, so becoming and having become are simultaneous in substantial change, and all the more in spiritual motion.

alalal-c49641-d1e395.summary: Rejects this as a strange philosophy at odds with all philosophers, who hold that nothing comes naturally from simple nothing and that becoming and having become are never simultaneous; substantial forms, admitting no more or less, make this even clearer. Others distinguish 'now', the indivisible substance of time, from 'instant', any point we signify between times, and say angels move in instants; Albert rejects this, since in that sense there is only one now in all time.
claims: Becoming and having become are never simultaneous, even in substantial change.

alalal-c49641-d1e480.summary: Further against the now-instant distinction: Averroes says one can take two points in a line but not in time, which neither persists nor has positioned parts; so Aristotle's claim that time lies between any two nows concerns nows terminating motion, and holds equally of instants, so the solution fails.

alalal-c49641-d1e517.summary: Solution: time is said in many ways. What is not related to the heavens' motion as cause is not in celestial time as numbered in number; Maimonides reduces all natural motion to the heavens, but angelic motion cannot be so reduced. Another time belongs to each mobile as its subject. Celestial time takes discreteness from before and after, continuity from space, and substance from the one moving thing. In the angel the mobile is indivisible and not commensurate with place, so there is no before and after from place, and the moving power overcomes spatial distance, so space does not make its motion continuous. There remain only three indivisibles, the one now of the angel taken three times, at the place from, through and to, with nothing continuing them.
claims: Angelic motion is not measured by celestial time, since it is not caused by the heavens.
Angelic motion consists of three discrete nows, at the terminus from, the place through, and the terminus to, without continuous time between them.

alalal-c49641-d1e633.summary: Reply to the first five arguments: those propositions hold only of physical motion, and angelic motion is neither physical nor ordered to the physical.
claims: Angelic motion is not physical motion.

alalal-c49641-d1e646.summary: Reply to the argument from intervening points: for an indivisible mover the whole intervening space is as one indivisible, so A and B are not divided by a point C; indivisibles divide only divisibles whose termini they are.
concepts: space as one indivisible for the angel

alalal-c49641-d1e668.summary: Reply to the two arguments about indivisibles and nows: they hold only of motion that derives continuity from space and makes time continuous, which angelic motion does not.

alalal-c49641-d1e688.summary: Against those who say the angel's moving and having moved are simultaneous in one now with two aspects, end of past and beginning of future: this cannot account for three termini, from, through and to. Their proof is false, since becoming and having become can never coincide. Averroes explains that generation and corruption never occur apart from alteration but are its terminus; motion has an end of the same genus and one of another genus, as generation ends alteration or illumination follows a moving light. So a thing is corrupted at the instant it is generated, as the end of motion, which is 'to' a now though not 'in' a now, as a line is to a point.
claims: Becoming and having become are never simultaneous; generation is the instantaneous terminus of alteration.
Motion is toward a now, not in a now, as a line terminates at a point.

alalal-c49641-d1e788.summary: Reply to the argument from simple generation: simple generation is not of being in general but of substance, whose subject is non-being only relative to the composite, i.e. matter in potency. Considered as generation of substance, matter alone is presupposed; as the corruption of another, matter with a departing form; as involving action and passion, matter with that form's contrary accidents. So becoming and having become are not simultaneous; corruption and generation coincide only relative to different forms, as end and beginning.
claims: Natural generation never proceeds from simple nothing; matter is always presupposed.

alalal-c49641-d1e877.summary: Notes that the question is difficult and has many opinions, some now held heretical by the moderns: Jewish philosophers such as Maimonides said angels 'move' only through powers obeying their nod, which contradicts Scripture; others said the angel is in many places at once, contrary to its definite substance; others that it moves in a now or in time at will; others in imperceptible time; others in one now under two aspects; and no two fully agree.
claims: It is heretical to hold that angels move only through obedient powers or are in many places at once.

alalal-c49641.summary: Article 24 asks whether angelic motion is in time or in the now. Eight arguments from Aristotle, Avicenna and Averroes hold that all motion has before and after, is successive, is divisible with space, and cannot consist of successive nows. Albert rejects two alternatives: that moving and having moved are simultaneous, modelled on a supposed generation from nothing, and that angels move in 'instants' rather than nows. His solution distinguishes kinds of time. Angelic motion is not caused by the heavens and so is not measured by celestial time. Its own time takes its character from its mobile and motion: the angel is indivisible and not commensurate with place, and its power overcomes distance, so its motion has no continuous before and after. It consists of three discrete nows, at the terminus from, the place through, and the terminus to. Physical principles do not apply. Becoming and having become are never simultaneous, since generation is the instantaneous terminus of alteration, toward a now but not in it. Albert surveys the diverse opinions, judging those of Maimonides and of multilocation heretical.
claims: Angelic motion is not measured by celestial time.
Angelic motion consists of three discrete successive nows: of departure, transit and arrival.
Becoming and having become are never simultaneous; generation is the terminus of alteration.
Views that angels move only through obedient powers, or are in several places at once, are heretical.
